title: Bargaining on the Shadow of the Law: Legal Frictions for Women Cross-Border Commuters Between Zimbabwe and South Africa
content: Cross-border commuting by women in low and middle-income countries remains severely under-researched, legally unrecognised, and wrongly merged into international migration data. This paper applies a four-step distributive analysis of the law to examine the legal frictions of stop and delay experienced by women cross-border commuters at the South Africa–Zimbabwe border. Drawing on qualitative fieldwork conducted in March 2025 in Musina and Johannesburg, including interviews with women commuters and civil society professionals, a focus group, border observation, and systematic legal mapping, the analysis identifies the primary norms generating frictions of stop and delay; the second-level norms from other bodies of law that compound their effects; the actors and interests the legal architecture structures; and the resulting distribution of costs and benefits. The paper makes three contributions. Methodologically, it demonstrates that the distributive analysis of the law offers mobilities scholarship a framework capable of tracing how formally neutral legal norms generate unequal outcomes across diverse groups of actors. Empirically and from a feminist mobilities perspective, it disaggregates women cross-border commuters into two analytically distinct sub-groups: documented women traders and undocumented women without capital, showing that legal costs, physical danger, and exposure to violence accumulate heterogeneously even within this category, while the benefits of crossing, including trade income, healthcare access, and relief from domestic violence, are real and survival-level for both. Theoretically, it advances a constitutive account of law within the politics of mobility, arguing that informal crossings, extortion networks, and survival trade are not produced outside the law but within a field of constraints and opportunities that law itself organises. Zimbabwe’s Statutory Instrument 59 of 2026 is identified as a recent legal development that materially worsens the distributional position of documented women traders, ignoring the underlying conditions that make cross-border trade necessary.
